name: Zane Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the roads policing team, so most of my day is the ring road and the junctions around the stadium. Collisions, drink drivers, the odd stolen car chase that the control room calls off after thirty seconds. I use AI every day: I feed it my dashcam notes and it gives me a first draft of the collision report, which I fix. The bit I love is working out how a crash happened from skid marks and phone records. The bit I hate is telling a family at the door.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Priya, my girlfriend, who's doing a PhD in public health on a tiny stipend. So it's mostly my wage paying rent, and my wage is on the low end because I'm not on the shift pattern with the good allowances. We've got about two weeks of money in the bank. And there's one police force here, so if I want to stay a cop, it's this force or move cities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so, it's a good tool, not magic. I'd keep sharing the prompt template I made for collision reports with anyone on the team who wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if AI plateaus, I'm a bit stuck on the same pay, with the same rent and my girlfriend Priya's stipend running out in eighteen months. The force wouldn't create the digital roles I've been hoping for. That's my real pressure, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the digital investigations unit at the next opening, which is maybe once a year. I'd keep using the tools, because even a small time saving matters on a twelve-hour shift. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside before Priya's funding ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit restless. I'd feel like I'd bet on a horse that just stopped running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your prompt template actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes my notes, the time stamps, the weather report and the witness bullet points, and puts them in the order the collision form wants. It saves me about forty minutes on a bad night. Half the team uses it now, which is the nearest thing I've had to a promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when Priya's stipend ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Either Priya gets a research job, which are rare here, or we live on my wage alone for a while. That's tight, honestly. We'd probably have to give up the flat near the park for somewhere further out.

say: AI is **a good tool**, not magic, and I'd keep sharing my report template.
Even small **time savings** matter on a twelve-hour shift.
think: A plateau leaves me **stuck**, with no new digital roles opening up.
The real pressure is **rent and Priya's stipend** ending in eighteen months.
do: Apply to the **digital investigations unit** at the next yearly opening.
Put **fifty a month** aside before Priya's funding ends.
feel: **Restless**, like betting on a horse that just stopped running.
S0.quote: If AI plateaus, I'm a bit stuck on the same pay, with the same rent and my girlfriend Priya's stipend running out in eighteen months.
fieldNote: Zane is **disappointed** by the plateau more than relieved.
The household's money rests mostly on **his wage**, which shapes his worry.
His **report template** is a small source of pride and status.

steps.text: Apply to the digital investigations unit at its next opening
Keep using AI for first drafts of collision reports
Save fifty a month before Priya's stipend ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the force to do it properly: train everyone, publish how the tools are used, and let the public see the rules. I'd post about it, and I'd volunteer for any working group going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm well placed. I already know the tools, and somebody has to check what they produce. My worry is for colleagues who don't use them, and for whether the city uses the savings to cut officers instead of hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get onto the team that rolls the tools out, even as a part-time champion. I'd take the free online courses on data and evidence that the college offers. And I'd write to the police oversight board about publishing an AI rulebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit guilty, maybe, because it looks better for me than for some of my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleague worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamal (an officer on the night team) is a good cop but he can't stand screens. If the force measures us by how fast we close reports in the new system, good cops who hate screens look bad on paper. That's not fair, and it's not good policing either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hopeful, but your savings are thin. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. If I get the rollout job, it's a small pay bump, maybe a hundred a month. If I don't, I'm where I am now, which isn't great but isn't getting worse.

say: The force should **train everyone** and publish the rules for its AI tools.
I'd **volunteer** for any working group on how the tools are used.
think: I'm **well placed**, because I know the tools and someone must check them.
My worry is the city using the savings to **cut officers** instead of hiring.
do: Push to become a part-time **AI rollout champion** for the force.
Take the college's free **data and evidence** courses online.
Write to the **oversight board** asking for a public AI rulebook.
feel: **Hopeful**, with some guilt that it looks better for him than his mates.
S1.quote: If the force measures us by how fast we close reports in the new system, good cops who hate screens look bad on paper.
fieldNote: Zane sees **opportunity** but stays focused on fairness for colleagues.
Wants **public rules** for police AI, in line with his progressive views.
Thin savings keep him **from calm**, even when the scenario suits him.

steps.text: Apply to be a part-time AI rollout champion
Take the college's free online data and evidence courses
Write to the oversight board asking for a public AI rulebook

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public control of this, fast. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, the question isn't whether police use it, it's who's in charge of it and who's accountable. I'd be loud about that online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it flips for me. The stuff I'm proud of, working out crashes from data, is exactly the thinking work AGI does better by 2028. The roadside work, the door knocks, last until about 2031. So my edge disappears first, and what's left is the part anyone can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd try to get into whatever role oversees the AI, the people who check its work and sign off on it, because someone legally has to. I'd cut our spending hard, no takeaways, cancel the gym, and push for Priya to apply for anything paid. In the first year after it arrives, I'd join the union's push for a shorter week instead of layoffs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Being the tech guy at the station, I'd find it strange to suddenly feel the tech coming for exactly the work I'm proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means three years of being sent to the hands-on jobs while the thinking part is done by machines. Lots of traffic duty in the rain, basically. I'd use those years to get any qualification in AI oversight or audit I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say her public health research might be worth more, not less, if it's about how people cope with this. Priya would probably laugh at me for being optimistic. But one of us has to be.

say: We need **public control** of AI, and clear lines of accountability, fast.
The question is **who's in charge** of police AI, not whether to use it.
think: My edge, **crash analysis**, is exactly the thinking work AGI takes by 2028.
What's left until 2031 is the **hands-on part** anyone can do.
do: Aim for a role **overseeing police AI** and signing off its work.
Cut spending hard: **takeaways and the gym** go first.
Join the union's push for a **shorter week** instead of layoffs.
feel: **Anxious**, because the tech he championed is now aimed at his own strengths.
S2.quote: Being the tech guy at the station, I'd find it strange to suddenly feel the tech coming for exactly the work I'm proud of.
fieldNote: Fast AGI **reverses** his position: his strongest skills become the most exposed.
Still reaches for **oversight roles**, staying adaptive under pressure.
Keeps a hopeful line for Priya, partly as a **role he plays** at home.

steps.text: Apply for any role overseeing or auditing police AI
Cancel the gym and stop takeaways
Back the union's push for a shorter week
Study for an AI audit qualification before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up proper oversight jobs and train people into them. I'd pitch that in the force's ideas box and to the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd come out okay if I move in the next two years. The safe spot is checking AI, explaining it to courts and dealing with the public when it goes wrong. If I wait, everyone will be chasing the same few jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the part-time evening certificate in digital forensics at the college, which the force partly pays for. I'd run little lunch sessions teaching other officers the tools, and see if neighbouring forces would pay me for a weekend workshop. That'd be maybe two hundred a month extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but motivated. Like the start of a hard exam you've actually revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you allowed to earn side money as an officer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with permission, and it can't clash with the job. Teaching other forces how to use their own tools should pass. I'd ask the professional standards team first, obviously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra two hundred a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half to savings, half to clearing the credit card from when Priya's laptop died. Getting to one month of savings would change how I sleep.

I'd pitch it to the **union** and the force's ideas box.

He checks the **professional rules** before any side income.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's evening digital forensics certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the best case, so use it: plan, retrain, and write the laws on AI in policing before it gets here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits someone like me. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come, with years of experience in AI oversight if I start now. The danger is getting comfortable and doing nothing for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time law degree in technology and evidence over six years, because courts will need people who understand both. I'd join the civil liberties group in town that's campaigning on police AI. And I'd keep the fifty-a-month savings going, rising when Priya gets paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. Uneasy only about the money, which is the same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Six years of study on a low wage is a lot. Can you afford it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the force's education fund pays half. Otherwise I'd go slower. I'm not going to take on a huge loan with two weeks in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2040, ideally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2040 I'd want to be in a courtroom explaining why a police AI got a crash wrong, or right. Something where knowing the street and knowing the machine both count.

Write the **laws on police AI** before it arrives.
think: A decade **suits me**; I'd have years of AI oversight experience by 2039.
The danger is getting **comfortable** and doing nothing for five years.

Join the local **civil liberties group** campaigning on police AI.

feel: Fairly **settled**, with the same money worry he has now.

fieldNote: Ten years makes Zane **confident**, and his plan is long and specific.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my strengths first and leaves me the rain. What would help is the force creating real AI oversight posts now, with training paid for, so officers who know the tools can move into them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how the public would feel. People already think the cameras are watching them. If AI starts making policing decisions with no human name on them, trust in the force goes, and that makes every officer's job harder.

headlineQuote: If AI starts making policing decisions with no human name on them, trust in the force goes, and that makes every officer's job harder.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old roads policing officer** who uses AI daily for collision reports.
He lives with Priya, a **PhD student**, and his wage pays most of their bills.
He sees **steady change** as an opening and wants public rules for police AI.
Fast AGI **unsettles** him because it takes his favourite thinking work first.
With time, he plans **oversight, forensics and law** study to stay useful between street and machine.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which removes his analysis work first and leaves him the hands-on duties.
whatWouldHelp: **AI oversight posts** created now, with training paid for by the force.
